_note: Hand-curated field guidance. NOT derived from iNaturalist data. Family entries are the fallback; taxon entries override them. Ripeness cues beat calendars every time - this file exists so the app tells you what to look at, not just when to look.
_schema: cue = how to tell it is ready | collect = technique | handling = after collection | caution = risk or legal note

Asteraceae.cue: Pappus (the fluff) has dried and begun to lift; heads look grey and open rather than green and tight.
Asteraceae.collect: Tug lightly - ripe achenes release with almost no resistance. If you have to pull, come back in a week.
Asteraceae.handling: Dries fast. Rub heads over a screen to separate achenes from chaff; many species have a high proportion of empty seed, so check fill by pinching.

Fabaceae.cue: Pods leathery to papery and turning brown; seeds rattle loose inside.
Fabaceae.collect: Many pods dehisce explosively - bag whole infructescences before they twist open, or check plants every few days.
Fabaceae.handling: Hard-coated seed benefits from scarification before sowing. Freeze or heat-treat to kill bruchid beetle larvae, which are common.

Poaceae.cue: Florets straw-coloured, seed firm; awns twist when dry.
Poaceae.collect: Strip the seed head upward through a closed hand into a bag. Ripe seed shatters readily - a light shake tells you.
Poaceae.handling: Keep well ventilated. Awned grasses tangle badly; leave awns on unless you are sowing with a drill.

Lamiaceae.cue: Calyces dry and brown, nutlets dark and hard inside.
Lamiaceae.collect: Bend the stalk over a bag and tap - ripe nutlets fall out cleanly.
Lamiaceae.handling: Winnow chaff gently; nutlets are small and blow away easily.

Rosaceae.cue: Varies with fruit type - fleshy fruits fully coloured and slightly soft, dry achenes brown and loose.
Rosaceae.collect: Pick fleshy fruit by hand; strip plumed achenes when they detach at a touch.
Rosaceae.handling: Clean pulp from fleshy fruit promptly - fermenting flesh kills seed. Most need cold-moist stratification.

Rhamnaceae.cue: Capsules turning from green to brown; a few on the plant have already popped.
Rhamnaceae.collect: Capsules explode when ripe, often within days. Bag branches or lay a sheet beneath and shake.
Rhamnaceae.handling: Dry in a paper bag - remaining capsules will fire and self-thresh. Most need heat and/or cold treatment to break dormancy.

Anacardiaceae.cue: Drupes fully coloured and firm; on sumacs the sticky coating has developed.
Anacardiaceae.collect: Strip clusters by hand. Watch that fruit persists long after ripening - old grey fruit from last season is often still attached.
Anacardiaceae.handling: Remove the fleshy or waxy coat. Hard seed coat usually needs scarification.
Anacardiaceae.caution: Confirm identity - this family includes poison oak, whose fruit is also collected by birds and looks superficially similar at a distance.

Fagaceae.cue: Acorn caps release cleanly and the nut is fully coloured; green acorns still tight in the cap are immature.
Fagaceae.collect: Collect from the ground within a day or two of drop, or pick mature acorns directly.
Fagaceae.handling: Float-test and discard floaters and any with weevil exit holes. Oak acorns are recalcitrant - they must not dry out. Sow promptly or refrigerate moist.

Ericaceae.cue: Berries fully coloured and slightly soft.
Ericaceae.handling: Macerate and float off pulp. Most require both scarification and stratification, and are slow and unreliable from seed.

Papaveraceae.cue: Capsule has gone from green to straw and the seed inside is dark, not pale.
Papaveraceae.collect: Capsules dehisce explosively. Bag them, or collect the moment the first few split.
Papaveraceae.handling: Dry fully in a paper bag; seed threshes itself as remaining capsules open.

Onagraceae.cue: Capsules dry and beginning to split at the tip.
Onagraceae.collect: Strip upward into a bag before the plumed seed disperses.
Onagraceae.handling: Screen out the fluff. Very small seed - use a fine sieve.

Polygonaceae.cue: Flower heads faded to rust or brown and papery; achenes dark and firm.
Polygonaceae.collect: Rub heads between palms over a bag.
Polygonaceae.handling: High chaff fraction is normal and mostly harmless for direct sowing.
Polygonaceae.caution: Buckwheats hold dried flower heads for months after seed has dropped, so a brown head is not proof of full seed.

Malvaceae.cue: Schizocarp segments brown and separating from the central axis.
Malvaceae.collect: Roll the disc gently between fingers - ripe segments break away.
Malvaceae.handling: Hard seed coat; scarify before sowing.

Boraginaceae.cue: Coils uncurled and dry, nutlets hard.
Boraginaceae.collect: Strip the uncurled coil into a bag.
Boraginaceae.handling: Nutlets shed easily and are often lost to timing - check plants frequently.

Apiaceae.cue: Umbels dry, mericarps brown and splitting into pairs.
Apiaceae.collect: Clip whole umbels into a bag.
Apiaceae.caution: This family includes poison hemlock and water hemlock, both lethally toxic. Do not collect from an umbellifer you have not identified with certainty.

Liliaceae.cue: Capsule dry, brown, and beginning to split; seed black and flat.
Liliaceae.collect: Tip the capsule into a bag - ripe seed pours out.
Liliaceae.handling: Easy to clean and store. Long juvenile period - expect years to flowering.

Adoxaceae.cue: Berries fully coloured, soft, and dropping.
Adoxaceae.collect: Hand-pick clusters. Birds strip these fast, so the window is short.
Adoxaceae.handling: Macerate and float off pulp within a day; fermentation kills the embryo.

Grossulariaceae.handling: Macerate, float off pulp, then cold-moist stratify.

Convolvulaceae.cue: Capsules papery and brown; seed hard and dark.

Lauraceae.cue: Fruit turns from green to purple-brown and softens.
Lauraceae.collect: Pick from the tree or gather fresh drop.
Lauraceae.handling: Remove flesh immediately. Recalcitrant - do not let dry, sow fresh.

Platanaceae.cue: Seed balls dry, brown, and starting to loosen into fluff.
Platanaceae.collect: Pick whole balls before they disintegrate.
Platanaceae.handling: Break apart over a bag; expect a lot of fluff and a low fill rate.

Salicaceae.collect: Collect the instant capsules open - viability is measured in days.
Salicaceae.handling: Sow immediately on wet mineral soil. Do not attempt to store.

Cactaceae.cue: Fruit fully coloured and slightly yielding.
Cactaceae.collect: Use tongs. Glochids are the real hazard, not the spines.

Heteromeles arbutifolia.cue: Pomes fully red and slightly soft. Orange-red is still immature.
Heteromeles arbutifolia.collect: Clip whole clusters. Fruit persists well past ripeness, so late in the season check that seed inside is plump and dark, not shrivelled.
Heteromeles arbutifolia.handling: Macerate and float off pulp. Cold-moist stratify 1-3 months. Fresh seed germinates readily.

Quercus agrifolia.cue: Acorn slips cleanly from the cap and is deep brown; the shell is hard.
Quercus agrifolia.collect: Gather from the ground during the first heavy drop, before weevils and rodents work through them.
Quercus agrifolia.handling: Float-test and discard floaters. Recalcitrant - never dry. Sow within weeks or store moist and cool.
Quercus agrifolia.caution: Acorn crops are strongly masting; some years produce almost nothing regardless of the modelled window.

Eschscholzia californica.cue: Long ribbed capsule turns straw-coloured and the seed inside is dark brown-black.
Eschscholzia californica.collect: Capsules fire explosively and the window is only a few days per capsule. Bag developing capsules or collect daily.
Eschscholzia californica.handling: Dry in a paper bag and let them self-thresh. No pretreatment needed.
Eschscholzia californica.caution: This species flowers and fruits nearly year-round in mild coastal sites, so the modelled window is much wider than any single population's.

Sambucus cerulea.cue: Berries fully blue with a waxy bloom, and soft.
Sambucus cerulea.collect: Clip whole umbels. Birds strip a plant in days once ripe.
Sambucus cerulea.handling: Macerate and float off pulp the same day. Warm then cold stratify.

Malosma laurina.cue: Drupes whitish and firm on a fresh cluster.
Malosma laurina.collect: Take only from current-season clusters - the plant holds grey, empty fruit from previous years all the way through winter and spring.
Malosma laurina.handling: Rub off the waxy coat, then scarify.
Malosma laurina.caution: This is the species that most badly misleads a calendar-based model. Persistent old fruit generates fruiting records year-round; judge by cluster condition, not by date.

Salvia mellifera.cue: Calyces brown and dry; nutlets dark and hard.
Salvia mellifera.collect: Bend stalks into a bag and tap. Ripe nutlets drop instantly.

Salvia apiana.cue: Flowering stalk fully dry and grey-brown; nutlets loose in the calyx.
Salvia apiana.collect: Strip the tall wands into a bag, or clip and invert.

Artemisia californica.cue: Flowering branchlets dry and grey; tiny achenes shed at a touch.
Artemisia californica.collect: Strip branchlets into a bag. The seed is minute - expect chaff to outweigh seed heavily.
Artemisia californica.handling: Do not over-clean; sow with the chaff.

Baccharis pilularis.cue: Female plants only - look for white pappus fluffing out of the heads.
Baccharis pilularis.collect: Strip fluff by hand once it lifts freely.
Baccharis pilularis.handling: Sow with pappus attached; separating it is more trouble than it is worth.
Baccharis pilularis.caution: Dioecious. Male plants never set seed, so half the plants you find are not collectible.

Eriogonum fasciculatum.cue: Heads rust-coloured; rubbing releases hard, dark, three-angled achenes.
Eriogonum fasciculatum.collect: Rub heads between palms over a bag and check that real seed is coming out, not just chaff.
Eriogonum fasciculatum.handling: Screening is optional for direct sowing.
Eriogonum fasciculatum.caution: Dried flower heads persist for months after the seed has already dropped. A brown head is not evidence of seed.

Adenostoma fasciculatum.cue: Flower clusters dry to rusty brown and achenes are firm.
Adenostoma fasciculatum.handling: Very small seed with a lot of chaff. Germination is erratic without fire-related cues such as smoke or charate treatment.

Rhus integrifolia.handling: Wash off the sticky exudate, then scarify. Slow and uneven to germinate.

Prunus ilicifolia.cue: Drupes fully dark red to purple-black and soft.
Prunus ilicifolia.collect: Hand-pick. Competition from wildlife is heavy.
Prunus ilicifolia.handling: Clean off flesh, then cold-moist stratify. Large seed, easy to handle and high viability.

Frangula californica.cue: Berries turn green to red to black; collect at full black and soft.
Frangula californica.collect: Hand-pick - fruit ripens unevenly, so expect several visits.

Umbellularia californica.cue: Fruit purple and slightly soft, often already on the ground.
Umbellularia californica.handling: Remove flesh at once and sow fresh - recalcitrant and short-lived.

Cercocarpus betuloides.cue: The long feathery plume is dry and fully twisted; the achene detaches at a light touch.
Cercocarpus betuloides.collect: Strip plumes into a bag on a still day - they carry off in any wind.

Epilobium canum.cue: Capsules splitting to reveal plumed seed.
Epilobium canum.collect: Bag capsules just as the first ones open.

Arctostaphylos glauca.handling: Clean pulp, then scarify and treat with heat or smoke. Manzanitas are notoriously difficult from seed; propagate from cuttings if you have the option.

Ceanothus.cue: Capsules darkening and the first few have already exploded.
Ceanothus.collect: Bag branch tips or lay a sheet - the window between ripe and gone can be under a week.
Ceanothus.handling: Dry in paper bags and let them self-thresh. Needs hot water followed by cold stratification.

Paeonia californica.cue: Follicles leathery and splitting; seed large, glossy, and blue-black.
Paeonia californica.collect: Open follicles by hand and tip the seed out.
Paeonia californica.handling: Sow fresh - do not let it dry. Complex dormancy and slow to establish.

Calochortus.cue: Capsule dry and papery, splitting along the seams; seed flat and dark.
Calochortus.handling: Easy to clean and store. Expect four or more years from seed to flower.
Calochortus.caution: Several Calochortus species are rare or narrowly endemic. Check status before collecting.

Platanus racemosa.cue: Seed balls brown and beginning to fray.
Platanus racemosa.collect: Pick balls from the tree before they break up.
Platanus racemosa.handling: Break apart over a bag. Fill rate is often low - check for plump achenes.

Malacothamnus.cue: Schizocarp segments brown and parting from the axis.

Comarostaphylis diversifolia.caution: CNPS rare-plant ranked and locally restricted. Enjoy it in place; seed collection from wild populations is not appropriate.
